one_liner: Offline optimal-parse LZ4 encoder whose standard LZ4 output decodes 1.45-1.54x faster than lz4 -12 output on enwik9.
what_it_does: lz4ultra is a compressor only: it writes ordinary LZ4 data (modern frames, legacy 8 MB frames, or raw blocks) that any LZ4 decoder reads, so the read side of a system needs no change. It ships as a C command-line tool with a library API underneath: lz4ultra_compress_inmem() and lz4ultra_decompress_inmem() for buffers, lz4ultra_compress_file() and lz4ultra_compress_stream() for files and streams, with flags for favor-ratio vs favor-decompression-speed, block size (64 KB to 4 MB), independent blocks, legacy frames and dictionaries. Its bundled decompressor exists mainly to verify output.
how_it_is_fast: The speedup comes from emitting fewer LZ4 tokens, not from a faster decoder: on enwik9 the favor-decSpeed output has 88.5 M tokens against 92.1 M for lz4 -12 --favor-decSpeed, and every token saved is one less branch-heavy step in the decoder. Matches are found with a suffix array (libdivsufsort) plus a wimlib-derived LCP-interval match finder, which enumerates all matches at each position. A backward dynamic-programming optimal parse then picks the cheapest token sequence, and a second pass merges or drops short matches to cut the command count. Favor-decSpeed mode adds a larger per-match penalty (5 instead of 1) so the parser prefers longer, fewer matches.
when_to_use: Compress-once, decompress-many assets (game data, firmware images, embedded or 8-bit platform payloads, read-only bundles) that are already read with a standard LZ4 decoder.
When you want lz4hc -12's ratio or slightly better but faster decoding, and offline compression time is irrelevant.
When the decoder cannot change (shipped hardware, third-party lz4 library) but you control the encoder.
Building a decode-speed-tuned LZ4 stream with --favor-decSpeed, which on enwik9 gave both a smaller file and a 1.54x faster decode than lz4 1.9.2 -12 --favor-decSpeed.
when_not_to_use: Any online or latency-sensitive compression path: it is an optimal parser over a suffix array, far slower than lz4 fast or lz4hc low levels (a WebSearch snippet of the smalLZ4 page lists lz4ultra 1.2.2 at 291 s for enwik9, about 3.4 MB/s).
Memory-tight encoders: the compressor allocates three 8-byte-per-position arrays over the block plus 64 KB of history (roughly 100 MB at the default 4 MB block) plus libdivsufsort working state.

When you need the reported gains confirmed on current tools: the comparison is against lz4 1.9.2 (2019) on one dataset, and lz4 1.10.0's lz4hc -12 already decodes silesia.tar at 3813 MB/s in lzbench 2.4.
When you only need ratio: smalLZ4 1.5 -9 reaches the same favor-ratio size (371,680,328 vs 371,680,323 bytes) and decode time on enwik9.
If you need a maintained dependency: last commit 2023-01-29, no tagged library releases, and the Makefile builds only the CLI.

integration.form: source-drop (Makefile builds the lz4ultra CLI only; the library API in src/lib.h has to be compiled into your project with bundled libdivsufsort and xxhash)
integration.dependencies: none external; bundles libdivsufsort (MIT) and xxhash
integration.min_toolchain: C99-era C; Makefile defaults to clang -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer; VS2017 and Xcode projects included
integration.platforms: any with a C compiler (POSIX, Windows via VS2017, macOS via Xcode); no SIMD requirement
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; each compress call builds its own lz4ultra_compressor context and the source shows no global mutable state, so separate calls on separate buffers should be independent.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — output is a drop-in for lz4 -12 output on the decode side, but the encoder API is lz4ultra's own, not LZ4_compress_HC()

gotchas: lz4ultra_compress_inmem() and lz4ultra_decompress_inmem() return size_t and signal errors with -1, so compare against (size_t)-1.

The README's decompression times do not say which decoder produced them; the tool's -dbench mode times lz4ultra's own decoder (best of 50 runs), which the README itself says is less optimized than lz4's.
Raw block mode (-r) is limited to 4 MB inputs and cannot store incompressible data (LZ4ULTRA_ERROR_RAW_UNCOMPRESSED).
The default is favor-ratio; the bigger decode-speed win needs --favor-decSpeed (or clearing LZ4ULTRA_FLAG_FAVOR_RATIO), which costs about 1.2% more output on enwik9.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over LZ4's own lz4hc when files are compressed once and decoded many times by an existing LZ4 decoder; pick zstd or LZSSE instead if you can change the decoder and want more ratio or decode speed, and plain LZ4 if compression speed matters.
verified_claims_summary: The author's README measures enwik9 on a Core i7-6700 (compiler and decoder build not stated): lz4ultra 1.3.0 --favor-decSpeed output decodes in 296,972 us against 457,141 us for lz4 1.9.2 -12 --favor-decSpeed output (1.54x, derived from page data) while also being smaller (376.1 MB vs 377.2 MB); in favor-ratio mode 347,936 us vs 505,804 us (1.45x) at 371.7 MB vs 372.4 MB. These are first-party numbers on one file with no published harness.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-01-29 (last commits were cppcheck and memory-leak fixes), but it is a small Zlib-licensed codebase with a CC0 match finder, and its output stays readable by any standard LZ4 decoder, so the encoder can be vendored for offline use.
